title: Relational Feature Caching for Accelerating Diffusion Transformers
claim: Output feature changes are irregular and hard to extrapolate, but input changes track them closely, so inputs can improve predictions and beat prior caching on efficiency and quality.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in one row, labeled (a)-(d) below; first two share axes, then error per module, then FLOPs vs quality tradeoff
description: A single row of four line charts with captions beneath: (a) Output difference, (b) Input difference, (c) Prediction error, (d) Performance. Panels (a) and (b) plot min-max normalized L2 distance against timestep, from about 45 down to 0, for the 10th (blue), 20th (gray) and 30th (red) modules. The jagged curves in (a) have nearly the same shape as those in (b), and both spike sharply at the end. Panel (c) plots relative L1 error against module index for FORA (green), TaylorSeer (orange) and Ours/RFC (blue). Ours is lowest through the middle modules. Panel (d) plots sFID against FLOPs. The blue RFC curve is low and nearly flat, below the orange TaylorSeer curve and the steeply falling green FORA curve. The eye goes first to the colored zigzag lines in (a) and (b).
caption: Feature analysis and comparison between existing approaches (FORA [ref], TaylorSeer [ref]), and our method (RFC) using DiT-XL/2 [ref]. (a-b) Min-max normalized $L_2$ distances of output and input features, measured between consecutive timesteps. While the variations of feature changes are irregular, those of input and output remain closely aligned with each other. (c) The prediction errors across different modules. We measure the relative $L_1$ error between output features with and without applying caching methods and average the values over the timesteps. (d) Quantitative results on ImageNet [ref] evaluated in terms of FLOPs and sFID [ref].
abstract: Feature caching approaches accelerate diffusion transformers (DiTs) by storing the output features of computationally expensive modules at certain timesteps, and exploiting them for subsequent steps to reduce redundant computations. Recent forecasting-based caching approaches employ temporal extrapolation techniques to approximate the output features with cached ones. Although effective, relying exclusively on temporal extrapolation still suffers from significant prediction errors, leading to performance degradation. Through a detailed analysis, we find that 1) these errors stem from the irregular magnitude of changes in the output features, and 2) an input feature of a module is strongly correlated with the corresponding output. Based on this, we propose relational feature caching (RFC), a novel framework that leverages the input-output relationship to enhance the accuracy of the feature prediction. Specifically, we introduce relational feature estimation (RFE) to estimate the magnitude of changes in the output features from the inputs, enabling more accurate feature predictions. We also present relational cache scheduling (RCS), which estimates the prediction errors using the input features and performs full computations only when the errors are expected to be substantial. Extensive experiments across various DiT models demonstrate that RFC consistently outperforms prior approaches significantly. Project page is available at https://cvlab.yonsei.ac.kr/projects/RFC
